jurisdiction.name: Seattle
jurisdiction.notes: City of Seattle, King County. Seattle is not a DOR Business Licensing Service partner city: the Seattle business license tax certificate is issued through FileLocal. Food permits and plan review come from Public Health – Seattle & King County, building and land use permits from SDCI, right-of-way permits (sidewalk cafes, vending) from SDOT. Seattle has no cabaret or entertainment license; nightlife is regulated through the liquor license review, the noise code, and the admission tax. The Secure Scheduling Ordinance (Office of Labor Standards) only applies to food service businesses with 500+ employees worldwide.

permits.name: Seattle Business License Tax Certificate (FileLocal)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Seattle Finance – License & Tax Administration
permits.notes: Required for almost every business operating in Seattle; apply on FileLocal (filelocal-wa.gov) once you have your UBI, because Seattle endorsements are not available through the state BLS. The 2026 fee is set by Seattle taxable revenue: $73 under $20k, $147 up to $500k, $667 up to $2M, $1,604 up to $5M, $3,210 above; businesses starting on or after July 1 pay half the Tier 1 fee in year one. Online, the certificate is printable 2–3 business days after payment; by mail, 1–6 weeks. Renew every year by December 31; SDOT vending and outdoor-dining permits ask for it.

permits.name: SDCI land use / zoning review (establish use; conditional use if not allowed outright)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI)
permits.notes: Moving into a space whose recorded use is not a restaurant or bar means establishing the new use through SDCI. It is usually folded into the construction permit; establishing use for the record alone is 1.5× the SDCI base fee. Restaurants and drinking establishments are generally allowed outright in Neighborhood Commercial (NC1–NC3) and Commercial zones, but subject to maximum size-of-use limits that are tightest in NC1, and pedestrian-designated ('P') zones control street-level frontage. If the use is not allowed outright you need a conditional use Master Use Permit, which SDCI says takes 4 to 8 months or more. Use SDCI's free 20-minute land use coaching and check the GIS zoning map before signing a lease.
permits.stall_risk: A use that needs a conditional use or other Master Use Permit adds 4–8+ months, including public notice and appeal periods. Confirm the zone, size limit and recorded use with SDCI coaching before you sign the lease, and make the lease contingent on land use approval.

permits.name: SDCI construction permit – addition/alteration (tenant improvement or change of use)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI)
permits.notes: Full plan review is needed for a change of use (for example bank to restaurant), new construction, or a kitchen build-out with a Type I hood. Start with the Building & Land Use Pre-Application in the Seattle Services Portal, then book an electronic intake; SDCI targets an initial review in 2–3 weeks for simple and about 8 weeks for complex projects, but final timing depends on correction rounds. Fees are based on project value (about 75% at submittal, the rest at issuance, plus a technology fee); electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits are pulled separately by trades. The permit is valid 18 months.
permits.stall_risk: Multiple correction cycles are the norm and each resubmittal goes back into the review queue. Use a Seattle-experienced architect, request a pre-submittal conference for complex projects, and submit the health plan review in parallel.

permits.name: SDCI subject-to-field-inspection (STFI) permit – minor interior alterations
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI)
permits.notes: The fast path for interior, non-structural alterations to an existing commercial space when the use is not changing (e.g. a cafe taking over a cafe). Screening takes a few days and the permit and stamped plans are issued electronically; an inspector reviews the work in the field instead of a plan reviewer. Fees are value-based. If the work grows to include a new hood, structural changes or a change of use, SDCI will route you to a full addition/alteration permit.

permits.name: Commercial kitchen hood permit (SDCI mechanical permit with Fire review)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI) with Seattle Fire Department review
permits.notes: Kitchen hood exhaust systems need an SDCI mechanical permit; include the Commercial Kitchen Hood Worksheet on a full-size sheet in the drawing set. Hood systems carry an extra fire review fee on top of value-based and hourly fees; SDCI says to plan for about 9 weeks on most projects (about 2–4 weeks initial review). Sprinkler work is a separate permit, and the hood's fire-suppression system must pass its acceptance test before the final inspection.

permits.name: Certificate of Occupancy (final SDCI and Fire inspections)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI)
permits.notes: Seattle only issues a new Certificate of Occupancy when the use (or number of residences) changes, so a restaurant replacing a restaurant normally gets a final 'approved' inspection instead. The CO follows passed final inspections, including Fire. The Seattle Fire Department will not issue an annual assembly occupancy permit without a copy of the CO, so schedule finals early.

permits.name: Seattle Fire Department assembly occupancy permit (annual)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Fire Department – Fire Marshal's Office
permits.notes: Required to operate an assembly occupancy with an occupant load of 100 or more (Seattle Fire Code 105.5.44). Occupant load counts standing room, so many bars and 50+ seat restaurants cross it. New applications must include a copy of the SDCI Certificate of Occupancy; an inspector visits, then the permit is mailed once fees are paid and it renews annually. A separate open-flame permit applies if you use candles in an assembly space.

permits.name: Public Health – Seattle & King County food establishment plan review
permits.issuing_agency: Public Health – Seattle & King County, Food & Facilities Program
permits.notes: Plans must be approved before construction, remodeling, or a change of ownership, so a new operator taking over an existing restaurant still files. Submit through the Public Health Permit Center with the plan review application and questionnaire; the 2026 fee is $1,008 for new construction (4-hour base) or $756 for a remodel/ownership change (3-hour base), plus $252/hour beyond the base. Public Health currently warns initial reviews can take 8–10 weeks. The emailed approval letter is what you use to apply for the operating permit.
permits.stall_risk: The 8–10 week initial review queue plus correction rounds on finish schedules, hand sinks and equipment specs is often the longest health item. Submit with SDCI on day one using the Plan Review and Permitting Guide and tip sheet, and answer reviewer emails within a day.

permits.name: Food business operating permit (Public Health – Seattle & King County)
permits.issuing_agency: Public Health – Seattle & King County, Food & Facilities Program
permits.notes: Apply in the Permit Center with your plan approval letter, pay the invoiced fee at least 10 business days before the pre-operational inspection, and book the inspection at least a week ahead. The 2026 annual fee depends on risk category and seats: $441 for Risk 1, $693–$945 for Risk 2, and $945–$1,386 for Risk 3 (full cooking), prorated by start quarter; the permit year runs April 1–March 31. Opening before passing the pre-op inspection can mean closure plus a fee of 50% of the annual permit.

permits.name: SPU fats, oils & grease (FOG) program – grease interceptor
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) – FOG program; King County Industrial Waste for large dischargers
permits.notes: Any business with commercial kitchen plumbing and a King County food permit must install and maintain a grease interceptor (SMC 21.16.310), including coffee shops, delis and pizza places. Discharge is capped at 100 ppm FOG, interceptors must be cleaned before they are 25% full, and enzymes or other additives are prohibited; fines run $250–$5,000. The interceptor is permitted and inspected as part of your plumbing/side-sewer work. Very large or process-heavy dischargers may also need a King County Industrial Waste discharge authorization. Keep pumping records on site.
permits.stall_risk: Finding room for an in-ground interceptor (and its lead time) in an older building often forces redesign late in plan review. Confirm the size and location with your plumber and SDCI before the plan set is final.

permits.name: SDCI sign, awning & canopy permit
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI)
permits.notes: Needed for any sign over 5 square feet or any illuminated or electrical sign (including neon or border tube lighting), and to install or re-cover an awning. Apply in the Seattle Services Portal; complete applications are usually issued in about a week. The base fee covers 32 sq ft with increments per extra 10 sq ft, plus electrical fees for lit signs. Historic districts (Pioneer Square, Pike Place) also need a board certificate of approval first.

permits.name: SDOT Street Use outdoor dining (sidewalk café / street café) permit
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) – Street Use / Public Space Management
permits.notes: Covers tables and chairs on the sidewalk, curb space or a street café in converted parking, made permanent by Council legislation in 2023. Choose a long-term permit (issuance, inspection and an annual renewal fee) or a seasonal one (April 1–October 31, issuance and inspection only; everything off the right-of-way by Oct 31). Applications go through the Seattle Services Portal and include a public notice with a 10-business-day comment period. Serving alcohol outside also requires adding the area to your WSLCB license.

permits.name: City of Seattle review of your WSLCB liquor application (local authority objection period)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle City Attorney's Office (precinct liaison attorneys) with SPD and City regulatory departments
permits.notes: No separate application: WSLCB notifies the City when you apply, and a precinct liaison attorney, SPD and City regulators review the applicant and location. The City has at least 20 days to recommend approval or object, extended to 60 days in an Alcohol Impact Area, and given volume it usually uses the full window. Objections rest on chronic illegal activity at the premises or your other licensed premises, patron conduct, prior criminal conduct, or your LCB violation history.
permits.stall_risk: A City objection sends the application to an LCB hearing and can add months. Contact the precinct liaison attorney and the SPD community police team before applying, especially for late-night bars or sites with a prior problem tenant.

permits.name: Noise code compliance & SDCI temporary noise variance (outdoor / off-hours amplified sound)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections (SDCI) – Noise Abatement Program
permits.notes: Seattle has no cabaret or entertainment license: indoor music and dancing are governed by the noise code (SMC 25.08, including the nightlife disturbance rule), your WSLCB license conditions, and admission tax if you charge a cover. You only need a temporary noise variance (up to 14 days, SDCI base fee, Services Portal) for outdoor amplified sound during quiet hours: 10 p.m.–7 a.m. weekdays, 10 p.m.–9 a.m. weekends. Neighbors must be notified 72 hours before. Soundproof and set a dB limit early, because noise complaints feed directly into liquor license renewals.

permits.name: Seattle admission tax endorsement (cover charges / ticketed events)
permits.issuing_agency: City of Seattle Finance – License & Tax Administration
permits.notes: Only needed if you charge a cover, ticket or minimum to enter. Seattle's admission tax is 5% of the full admission charge, and you need the admission tax endorsement on your business license before the first paid-entry event. Live-music venues can qualify for an exemption certificate: under 1,000 capacity with live music at least 3 days and 16 performances a week, or 500 or fewer with at least 2 days a week, plus regular reports.

permits.name: Seattle hotel employee protection ordinances (SMC 14.26–14.29) compliance
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Office of Labor Standards (OLS)
permits.notes: Seattle has no separate hotel license; a hotel needs the general business license plus lodging-tax reporting through DOR. Since July 1, 2020, four ordinances that replaced Initiative 124 govern hotel employers (coverage generally starts at about 60 rooms; confirm thresholds in the OLS Q&A). They require panic buttons, guest-room signage and violent-guest policies (SMC 14.26), injury protections, job retention on sale, and monthly health-care expenditures for larger hotels (SMC 14.28: $612–$1,837 per employee per month in 2026). There is no permit to file, but OLS enforces through complaints and investigations, so have the policies and panic-button program in place before opening.

permits.name: King County commissary & restroom use agreements (mobile food)
permits.issuing_agency: Public Health – Seattle & King County (approved commissary kitchen operator)
permits.notes: A mobile food unit plan review must include a signed Use of Commissary Agreement and Use of Restroom Agreement. Pick a kitchen from King County's approved commissary map (commercial commissaries have been permitted directly by Public Health since April 2025) and confirm it fits your prep, storage and water/waste needs. Commissary rent is a private cost, typically several hundred dollars a month; changing commissaries later costs $25.

permits.name: King County mobile food unit plan review & operating permit
permits.issuing_agency: Public Health – Seattle & King County, Food & Facilities Program
permits.notes: Submit plans for the truck or cart through the Public Health Permit Center using the Mobile Food Unit Plan Review and Permitting Guide; initial reviews currently take up to 8–10 weeks. The 2026 annual operating fee is $630 (Risk 1), $1,008 (Risk 2) or $1,260 (Risk 3), billed separately from the plan review fee; units already permitted by another Washington county can skip the plan review fee through reciprocity. Pass the pre-operational inspection before your first service.

permits.name: Seattle Fire Department food vending permit (propane / solid fuel, WSAFM truck inspection)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Fire Department – Fire Marshal's Office
permits.notes: Required to use propane, CNG or charcoal for food vending (Seattle Fire Code 105.5.32). Seattle uses the Washington State Association of Fire Marshals food truck inspection, held Wednesday mornings and booked when you apply and pay; a WSAFM decal from another participating jurisdiction can earn a discounted permit. Trucks also need an annual fuel-gas piping inspection from a qualified provider. Apply by emailing the 8206 forms to permits@seattle.gov.

permits.name: SDOT street food vending permit (curb, sidewalk/plaza, or route)
permits.issuing_agency: Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) – Public Space Management
permits.notes: Needed to vend from curb space, a sidewalk or plaza, or on a route in the public right-of-way (private lots need the property owner's OK instead). Apply in the Seattle Services Portal with your Seattle business license, Public Health permit, Fire permit if you cook with propane, photos of the unit and a site plan; fees are due within 30 days of approval. The vending year runs February 1–January 31: renew between November 1 and 30 to keep location priority, and unrenewed spots go to a lottery in early January.
